title: Intervals
sub: Merging after sorting by start, inserting in O(n), greedy by end, and a sweep for a timeline of buffs and sounds
cards/0/title: Merge Intervals: the problem and the signals
cards/0/body:
Merge Intervals (LeetCode #56). You get an array of intervals [start, end]. Merge all overlapping ones and return non-overlapping intervals that cover the same points. n ≤ 10⁴, endpoints from 0 to 10⁴. The intervals are closed: [1, 4] and [4, 5] share the point 4 and merge into [1, 5].

Signals of the interval family: the input is "start — end" pairs (times, ranges, segments on an axis), and the question is to merge, insert, remove the fewest, or count how many overlap at once. The reflex is to sort: by start (merge, insert) or by end (pick as many non-overlapping ones as possible).

When two intervals overlap. It is easier to say when they do not: one ended before the other started. Negating that gives the condition: a.start ≤ b.end and b.start ≤ a.end. For half-open [start, end) it is the same with strict signs: touching [1, 4) and [4, 5) is no longer an overlap. Time in games is usually half-open: a buff from second 10 lasting 5 seconds is [10, 15), and at 15 it is gone. Ask which convention applies at the start.
cards/1/q: Do the intervals [5, 9] and [2, 5] overlap as closed intervals? And [5, 9) and [2, 5) as half-open ones?
cards/1/options/0: Closed — yes, they share the point 5; half-open — no
cards/1/explain: Closed: 5 ≤ 5 and 2 ≤ 9 — both conditions hold, the point 5 belongs to both. Half-open: you need 5 < 5, which is false: [2, 5) ends exactly where [5, 9) begins and does not contain 5.
cards/1/wrong/1: For half-open intervals the signs are strict: 5 < 5 does not hold. [2, 5) does not contain the point 5.
cards/1/wrong/2: The closed ones do share the point 5: 5 ≤ 5 and 2 ≤ 9.
cards/1/wrong/3: The other way round: closing adds the endpoints, so closed intervals overlap at least wherever half-open ones do.
cards/2/title: The idea: after sorting by start, only the last block matters
cards/2/body:
Naively you merge any two overlapping intervals while such a pair exists: one pass over the pairs is O(n²), and there can be up to n passes. With n = 10⁴ that is 10⁸ checks per pass — too expensive.

What sorting by start buys. Overlapping intervals end up next to each other. If the next interval starts after the end of the current block, so do all later ones: their starts are no smaller. So you only ever compare with the last block of the result.

Invariant: res holds non-overlapping blocks in ascending order; all but the last are final, and the last can still grow. On an overlap, extend the last block to the max of the ends: an interval may lie entirely inside the block and must not shorten it. No overlap — open a new block. Time O(n log n) for the sort plus O(n) for the pass, O(n) memory for the answer. res[^1] is the last element, an index from the end (C# 8, works in Unity).

In a game: shield durations during a fight — "for how many seconds was at least one shield active" is the total length of the merged blocks; occupied ranges on a sound track; invulnerability windows from several sources.
cards/2/deep:
Why it is correct. Let the intervals be sorted by start, and let the current block [S, E] be the union of intervals 0 through i−1 of this run. If start_i > E, every later interval has start ≥ start_i > E — none of them touches what is already collected, and the block is closed for good. If start_i ≤ E, interval i overlaps the block and the union is [S, max(E, end_i)]. Induction on i.

Without allocations. You can write the answer straight into the sorted array: keep the index k of the last block, on a new block do a[++k] = a[i], and at the end the first k + 1 elements are the answer. O(1) memory on top of the sort.

Not an array of arrays. An int[][] is n separate heap objects and a sort with a delegate. In your own code, keep intervals as struct Interval { public int Start, End; } or as two arrays starts and ends — then Array.Sort(starts, ends) from the previous lesson sorts by start with direct comparisons while the ends ride along. In Burst — a NativeArray of structs and a struct comparer.
cards/3/q: Assemble Merge Intervals. Here the endpoints can be any int values, not just 0..10⁴.
cards/3/explain: Sort by start with CompareTo: the difference a[0] − b[0] overflows on endpoints like int.MinValue and 1 and gets the wrong sign. The intervals are closed and touching ones merge: ≤. The block end is the max of the two: [4, 5] inside [1, 6] must not shorten the block to 5. And res gets a copy, new[] { iv[0], iv[1] }: otherwise extending a block would silently modify the input array.
cards/4/task: Step through the trace on [2, 6] [1, 3] [8, 10] [4, 5] [12, 15] [9, 12]. The rig first sorts the intervals by start, then stops twice and asks what happens to the last block.
cards/4/goal/asks/0/q: The last block is [1, 6]. The next interval is [4, 5]. What does the code do?
cards/4/goal/asks/0/explain: 4 ≤ 6 — an overlap, so the last block is extended. But [4, 5] lies entirely inside [1, 6]: max(6, 5) = 6, and the block does not change. Had the end simply been assigned, the block would shrink to [1, 5] and lose the point 6.
cards/4/goal/asks/1/options/1/label: A new block [12, 15] opens: they only touch
cards/4/goal/asks/1/q: The last block is [8, 12]. The next one is [12, 15]. What does the code do?
cards/4/goal/asks/1/explain: The intervals are closed: the point 12 is in both, and iv[0] <= res[^1][1] holds. The block grows to [8, 15]. With half-open intervals the condition would be strict and [12, 15) would open a new block — which is why you ask about the convention up front.
cards/5/title: Insert Interval (#57): inserting in O(n) without sorting
cards/5/body:
The problem. The intervals are already sorted by start and do not overlap. Insert a new [s, e] and merge where needed. Appending it and calling Merge costs O(n log n) for the sort, even though the order is already there. One pass in three phases is enough:

1. Entirely to the left: the interval's end is strictly less than s — copy it as is.
2. Overlapping or touching: its start is ≤ e — absorb it: s = min(s, start), e = max(e, end).
3. Add [s, e] and copy everything left — it is entirely to the right.

The signs are where people slip: the intervals are closed and touching ones merge, so phase 1 uses a strict < and phase 2 a non-strict ≤. Time O(n), O(n) memory for the answer. You can find the phase boundaries with binary search in O(log n), but copying is still O(n).

In a game: a character holds a sorted list of windows during which an effect is active; a new application arrives — insert with merging instead of re-sorting the whole list. The example from the code runs on the rig next.
cards/6/task: Step through inserting [4, 8] into [1, 2] [3, 5] [6, 7] [8, 10] [12, 16] — the example from the code. The rig stops twice and asks which phase an interval falls into: compare its ends with s and e on screen.
cards/6/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Copy it as left: its start 3 < s = 4
cards/6/goal/asks/0/q: s = 4, e = 8, [1, 2] is already in res. Next is [3, 5]. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/0/explain: Phase 1 looks at the end, not the start: 5 < 4 is false, so [3, 5] is not entirely to the left. Phase 2 checks the start: 3 ≤ 8 — it overlaps the new interval, so we absorb it: s = min(4, 3) = 3, e = max(8, 5) = 8. Had the code compared the start with s, [3, 5] would go to the answer on its own and overlap [3, 8].
cards/6/goal/asks/1/q: The new interval has grown to [3, 8]. Next is [8, 10]. What does the code do?
cards/6/goal/asks/1/explain: The intervals are closed and point 8 belongs to both — touching merges. The phase 2 condition is non-strict: ivs[i][0] <= e, 8 ≤ 8, and e = max(8, 10) = 10. With a strict < the answer would hold [3, 8] and [8, 10] side by side, though they are one block. The next one, [12, 16], starts after 10 — phase 2 ends and [3, 10] goes into res.
cards/7/q: With ivs = [[1, 2], [5, 6]] and add = [2, 4] this code returns [[1, 2], [2, 4], [5, 6]], but the answer is [[1, 4], [5, 6]]. Tap the line with the bug.
cards/7/explain: Phase 1 copies intervals that end before the new one starts. With ≤, [1, 2] gets in too: its end 2 equals s = 2, the intervals touch and by the problem statement must merge. It needs a strict ivs[i][1] < s — then [1, 2] goes to phase 2 and s becomes 1.
cards/8/body:
The problem. What is the minimum number of intervals to remove so that the rest do not overlap? Here touching does not count as overlapping: [1, 2] and [2, 3] coexist. Removing the fewest is the same as keeping the most pairwise non-overlapping intervals: the classic scheduling problem — one meeting room, as many meetings as possible.

The greedy choice: sort by end and take the interval that ends first; skip everything that starts before its end; repeat. The earlier it ends, the more room is left for the rest.

Why not by start. [1, 100], [2, 3], [4, 5]: by start you take [1, 100] first and throw out both others, while by end you keep [2, 3] and [4, 5] and remove one. Nor by length: [1, 5], [4, 7], [6, 10] — the shortest, [4, 7], blocks both neighbours, while by end you keep two. The rigorous proof — an exchange argument — is in the fourth lesson.

The code: end is the end of the last kept interval. A start ≥ end — keep it and move the line, otherwise remove it. O(n log n), O(1) memory on top of the sort. In a game: one announcer voice channel — as many lines as possible without overlap.
cards/8/deep:
Arrows and balloons (#452, Minimum Number of Arrows to Burst Balloons): balloons are intervals, and an arrow at point x bursts every balloon containing it. The minimum number of arrows is the same greedy: by end, shoot at the end of the first one, skip everything that starts no further right than that point. The difference from #435 is that touching counts here (an arrow at a shared point bursts both), so a new shot needs a strict start > arrow.

When greedy by end fails. If meetings have weights (a payoff) and you maximize the total rather than the count, the earliest end can crowd out one expensive meeting. That is DP: sort by end, for each meeting binary-search the last compatible one and take max(take, skip) — O(n log n). DP is in the backtracking and dynamic programming unit.

Why int.MinValue instead of the first interval. A starting line at "minus infinity" guarantees the first interval by end is taken and removes a separate branch for an empty array.
cards/9/task: Step through the trace on [1, 3] [2, 4] [3, 5] [1, 2] [5, 7] [4, 6]. The rig sorts the intervals by end and asks once what the code will do. Touching is not an overlap here.
cards/9/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: Keep it: 2 ≥ 2, the line moves to 4
cards/9/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: Remove it: its start 2 equals the line
cards/9/goal/asks/0/q: [1, 2] is kept and the line is at 2; [1, 3] has been removed. The next by end is [2, 4]. What does the code do?
cards/9/goal/asks/0/explain: [2, 4] starts exactly where [1, 2] ended — that is touching, and in this problem touching does no harm. iv[0] >= end: 2 ≥ 2 — keep it, the line moves to 4. Later [4, 6] is kept the same way (4 ≥ 4), while [3, 5] and [5, 7] start before the line and go: 3 removed, 3 kept.
cards/10/title: Unity: a timeline of buffs and sounds — the sweep
cards/10/body:
A timeline raises two different questions.

"For how many seconds was at least one buff active?" — merge the intervals as in Merge Intervals and add up the block lengths. An overlap of two buffs is not counted twice.

"How many sounds play at once at the peak?" (Meeting Rooms II, #253 — how many meeting rooms you need). This is a sweep: walk through time, each start is +1, each end is −1, and the answer is the maximum of the running sum. It is convenient to keep starts and ends in two sorted arrays and move two pointers over them. The subtlety is equal times: sounds are half-open [start, end), and a sound that ends at 2 does not overlap one that starts at 2. So at equal times ends are processed before starts — in the code that is e[j] <= s[i]. O(n log n).

Why this matters in Unity. The peak of simultaneous sounds is the size of your AudioSource pool: fewer and sounds get cut off, more and you hold idle objects. The engine has its own limit too: Max Real Voices in Project Settings → Audio, 32 by default; beyond it Unity makes voices virtual — the quietest and lowest-priority ones go silent.
cards/11/task: Step through the sweep for the sounds [0, 3) [1, 2) [2, 5) [3, 4). The rig calls them meetings and the AudioSources rooms R1, R2: a source whose sound has ended goes back to the pool and serves the next one. The counter is how many play right now, its peak is the pool size. The rig stops where an end and a start fall on the same time.
cards/11/goal/asks/0/options/0/label: The end of [1, 2) first: 1 plays, R2 is free
cards/11/goal/asks/0/options/1/label: The start of [2, 5) first: 3 play, a new peak
cards/11/goal/asks/0/q: [0, 3) and [1, 2) are playing, the peak is 2. At time 2, [1, 2) ends and [2, 5) starts. What does the code handle first?
cards/11/goal/asks/0/explain: At equal times ends go before starts: the sounds are half-open, and [1, 2) is already silent at time 2. The counter drops to 1, R2 is freed, and [2, 5) takes it — the peak stays 2. Handling the start first would count three sounds at once and add a spare AudioSource to the pool. At time 3 the same happens with [0, 3) and [3, 4): the peak never goes above 2.
cards/12/q: Merge Intervals in an interview, out loud. Put the steps of the explanation in order.
cards/12/items/0: Clarify: closed or half-open intervals, does touching merge, is the input sorted, may I modify the array
cards/12/items/1: Naive: merge pairs while overlaps remain — O(n²) per pass
cards/12/items/2: The idea: after sorting by start, an interval can only overlap the last block
cards/12/items/3: Code it, stating the invariant: blocks in res do not overlap, only the last one grows
cards/12/items/4: Run [1, 3] [2, 6] [4, 5] [8, 10] — an interval inside a block
cards/12/items/5: Complexity: O(n log n) time, O(n) for the answer
cards/12/items/6: Edge cases: one interval, everything merges into one, touching endpoints, nested intervals
cards/12/explain: First of all, the boundary convention: the sign in the condition depends on it. The example with [4, 5] inside [1, 6] checks the max when extending, and touching endpoints check that very sign.
cards/13/q: Match the question with the technique.
cards/13/pairs/0/1: By start, extend the last block
cards/13/pairs/1/1: Three phases in O(n), no sorting
cards/13/pairs/2/0: Remove the fewest so none overlap
cards/13/pairs/2/1: By end, take the one ending first
cards/13/pairs/3/0: How many AudioSources the pool needs
cards/13/pairs/4/0: Seconds with at least one buff active
cards/13/pairs/4/1: Merge, then add up the lengths
